options.text: The argument holds, because the Mexica and Inca had no armies of their own.
options.misconception: The Mexica and Inca had large, organized armies; the claim about them is false.

options.text: The argument holds, because Spanish armies killed most Native peoples in battle.
options.misconception: Warfare was brutal, but battles could not kill half to nine-tenths of a hemisphere.

options.text: The argument fails, because disease killed on a scale warfare could not reach.
The argument fails, because no Native peoples died from disease at all.
options.misconception: Disease was the main killer; saying none died from it is the opposite of the evidence.

rationales.general:
1. Do the math of a hemisphere. Fifty to ninety percent of a hemisphere cannot die in battle alone.
2. Weigh the causes. Disease struck whole towns at once, far from any battlefield.
3. Check the armies. The Mexica and Inca had large, organized forces; they lost to disease and allies as much as to steel.
4. Rule out the extremes. Warfare mattered, but it could not reach the scale of the epidemics.
Remember: when a death toll spans a hemisphere, look for a cause that spans a hemisphere.
rationales.C: Disease struck whole towns at once, far from any battlefield, on a scale warfare could not reach.
rationales.A: The Mexica and Inca had large, organized armies. The claim about them is false.
rationales.B: Warfare was brutal, but battles could not kill half to nine-tenths of a hemisphere.
rationales.D: Disease was the main killer. Saying none died from it is the opposite of the evidence.

stem: Historians estimate that between 50 and 90 percent of the Native peoples of the Americas died between 1500 and 1650. A student argues that warfare alone explains this loss. Which response best evaluates that argument?

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of a Nahua account in the Florentine Codex (16th century), public domain; compiled by Bernardino de Sahagun with Nahua scholars.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of a Nahua account of smallpox in Tenochtitlan, recorded in the Florentine Codex, compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun with Nahua scholars in the 1500s. The account describes the sick lying in their houses and sleeping places, no longer able to move or stir, while the healthy could not bury the dead fast enough. Whole neighborhoods fell ill at once.
